title: Burgundy Level 3 Comprehensive Assessment Question Bank

questions.question: What is the ideal slope aspect for Burgundy's top vineyards?
options: East or southeast, for gentle morning sun
questions.explanation: East- or southeast-facing slopes provide gentle morning sun while avoiding excessive afternoon exposure, and ensure good drainage — the ideal orientation for Burgundy's top vineyards.

questions.question: What is the most distinctive feature of the Kimmeridgian soil in Chablis's Grands Crus?
questions.explanation: Kimmeridgian soil formed in the late Jurassic and is rich in small oyster fossils (Exogyra virgula), giving Chablis white wine its distinctive minerality and briny character.

questions.question: Within the Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru, what is the main difference between the upper- and lower-slope plots?
options: More clay upslope, more limestone downslope
More limestone upslope, producing elegance; more clay downslope, producing richer wines
No noticeable difference — quality is consistent
The lower slope is always better quality
questions.explanation: Clos de Vougeot's upper slope (near Musigny) has more limestone, producing elegant, refined wines; the lower slope has more clay, producing richer, fuller wines — which is also why prices within this single Grand Cru can differ by more than fivefold.

questions.question: Climate change has pushed Burgundy's harvest dates about 2 weeks earlier on average.
questions.explanation: Burgundy's average temperature has risen about 1.5°C over the past 30 years, and the harvest has moved from late September in the 1980s to early September today — an average of about 2 weeks earlier.

questions.question: Why is Pinot Noir considered the variety that most faithfully expresses terroir?
options: Extremely high-yielding and easy to grow
Extremely sensitive to its environment, precisely expressing terroir differences
questions.explanation: Pinot Noir is extremely sensitive to its environment — the same variety, planted in plots only 100 meters apart, can produce dramatically different wines. This extreme sensitivity makes it a "transparent translator" of terroir.

questions.question: What style of wine does limestone-dominant soil typically produce?
questions.explanation: Limestone soil drains extremely well and typically produces light-bodied, distinctly mineral, high-acid, elegant wines — such as Musigny and Montrachet.

questions.question: Why are Chambolle-Musigny's wines especially elegant and refined?
options: A special winemaking technique is used
It sits in a bowl-shaped amphitheater with forest protection and thin, poor soil
A special Pinot Noir clone is used
questions.explanation: Chambolle-Musigny sits in a natural amphitheater shape; a forest barrier on the east shields it from cold winds, and the soil is a thin layer of limestone that forces roots deep — producing extremely elegant wines.

questions.question: Burgundy uses only Pinot Noir and Chardonnay so as to purely express each plot's unique terroir.
questions.explanation: Using a single variety eliminates blending as a variable, purely expressing each plot's uniqueness — the biggest difference between Burgundy's philosophy and Bordeaux's blending tradition.

questions.question: For every 100-meter rise in elevation, roughly how much does temperature drop?
questions.explanation: Temperature drops about 0.6°C for every 100 meters of elevation gain — an important factor affecting grape ripeness and acidity.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among Burgundy producers' strategies for coping with climate change?
options: Increasing leaf canopy to shade the grapes
Reassessing the potential of high-altitude plots
questions.explanation: Burgundy has traditionally not used irrigation, relying on natural rainfall. Producers mainly cope with climate change by adjusting harvest timing, canopy management, and plot selection.

questions.question: Which is DRC's only white-wine Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: DRC holds 0.67 hectares of Montrachet, the estate's only white-wine Grand Cru — produced in tiny quantities and at very high prices.

questions.question: Domaine Leroy's founder, Lalou Bize-Leroy, targets roughly what yield per hectare?
questions.explanation: Leroy practices extreme biodynamic viticulture with very low yields — only 15-18 hl/ha, far below the legal maximum — the source of its wines' concentration.

questions.question: Domaine Armand Rousseau is considered the most representative estate in the village of Gevrey-Chambertin.
questions.explanation: Armand Rousseau holds several top plots in Gevrey-Chambertin, including Chambertin and Clos de Bèze, making it the village's most respected estate.

questions.question: Roughly what proportion of new oak does Domaine Coche-Dury use?
questions.explanation: Coche-Dury uses only 20-30% new oak, avoiding wood flavors masking terroir expression — one reason its whites are so pure and elegant.

questions.question: What proportion of the Musigny Grand Cru does Domaine Comte de Vogüé own?
questions.explanation: Vogüé holds 7.12 of Musigny's 7.2 hectares — about 70% — making it Musigny's largest landholder.

questions.question: Which winemaker, hailed as the greatest Burgundy winemaker of the 20th century, profoundly shaped Méo-Camuzet's style?
questions.explanation: Henri Jayer is regarded as one of the 20th century's greatest Burgundy winemakers. He mentored Jean-Nicolas Méo in establishing Méo-Camuzet's winemaking style.

questions.question: Both DRC and Domaine Leroy use 100% whole-cluster fermentation.
questions.explanation: DRC uses 100% whole-cluster fermentation, but Leroy adjusts the proportion depending on the vintage and plot — it isn't always 100%.

questions.question: What is Domaine Dujac's typical whole-cluster fermentation proportion?
questions.explanation: Dujac is a firm advocate of 100% whole-cluster fermentation; Jacques Seysses believes it brings greater complexity and spice character.

questions.question: During which period did Domaine Comte de Vogüé undergo a quality revolution and return to the top ranks?
questions.explanation: After François Millet took over in 1986 and reformed the estate, quality improved markedly starting with the 1990 vintage, returning the domaine to the top ranks.

questions.question: Which estate's Meursault Les Perrières is considered comparable in quality to a Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Coche-Dury's Meursault Les Perrières is considered by many experts to rival Le Montrachet in quality — one of the finest Premier Cru whites in Burgundy.

questions.question: Which vintage is considered the 21st century's first perfect vintage?
questions.explanation: 2005 is widely recognized as the 21st century's first perfect vintage — ideal climate conditions produced wines that are concentrated, balanced, and have excellent aging potential.

questions.question: In 2003, extreme heat led to many wines with excessive alcohol and insufficient acidity.
questions.explanation: 2003 was one of the hottest vintages on record; many wines exceeded 14% alcohol and lacked acidity, losing Burgundy's classic elegance.

questions.question: What was the main issue with the 2021 vintage?
options: Severe frost causing very low yields
questions.explanation: 2021 suffered severe frost damage, with yields down 30-50%, though the surviving grapes were of excellent quality.

questions.question: For a 2019 Grand Cru red wine, what is roughly the ideal drinking window?
questions.explanation: 2019 is an excellent vintage with Grand Cru aging potential up to 50 years; the ideal drinking window is 2025-2050.

questions.question: 1999 is considered a seriously underrated excellent vintage.
questions.explanation: 1999 is often overshadowed by 1990 and 2000, but is actually an excellent vintage with reasonable prices and outstanding value.

questions.question: Which factor has the least influence on a Burgundy wine's aging potential?
questions.explanation: Acidity, tannin structure, and the producer's winemaking skill all directly determine aging potential; cork quality, though important, mainly affects storage stability rather than the wine's own aging architecture.

questions.question: What characterizes the 2010 vintage?
options: Early-maturing, richly fruity, ready to drink early
Powerful structure, high acidity, needs long aging
questions.explanation: 2010 has powerful structure and high acidity — a classic vintage for long-term aging.

questions.question: In difficult vintages, top producers can usually still make good wine.
questions.explanation: Top producers have superior vineyard management and winemaking skill, allowing them to make excellent wines even in difficult vintages through rigorous selection and technical adjustments.

questions.question: White wine's ideal aging period is typically ___ than red wine's.
questions.explanation: Burgundy white wine's aging potential is generally shorter than red — typically peaking at 10-20 years, while top red wine can age 30-50 years.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of buying En Primeur (wine futures)?
options: The price is usually lower and it secures an allocation
questions.explanation: The advantage of buying En Primeur is a lower price than the market and a secured allocation, but it requires paying upfront and waiting 2-3 years for delivery.

questions.question: In which geological era did Burgundy's soils mainly form?
questions.explanation: Burgundy's soils mainly formed during the Jurassic period (200-145 million years ago), when the region was a warm, shallow sea.

questions.question: What is the most distinctive feature of Kimmeridgian soil?
questions.explanation: Kimmeridgian soil is rich in small oyster fossils (Exogyra virgula) — the signature feature of Chablis's Grands Crus.

questions.question: All seven of Chablis's Grands Crus sit on Kimmeridgian soil.
questions.explanation: All seven of Chablis's Grands Crus sit on the right bank of the Serein river on Kimmeridgian soil — the foundation of their exceptional quality.

questions.question: What is the main soil difference between the Côte de Nuits and the Côte de Beaune?
options: The Côte de Nuits has more clay, the Côte de Beaune more limestone
The Côte de Nuits has more limestone, the Côte de Beaune more clay
Their soils are exactly the same
The Côte de Nuits is granite
questions.explanation: The Côte de Nuits is mainly limestone mixed with red clay (suiting Pinot Noir), while the Côte de Beaune is mainly white marl and limestone (suiting Chardonnay).

questions.question: What is the ideal soil pH range in Burgundy?
questions.explanation: Burgundy's ideal soil pH is between 7 and 8 (slightly alkaline), which helps preserve high grape acidity and nutrient availability.

questions.question: Iron content in the soil affects a wine's aromatic development.
questions.explanation: Iron affects grape metabolism and aromatic development; iron-rich soils (such as at Romanée-Conti) often contribute a "bloody" and mineral character.

questions.question: Roughly how deep is the soil at Le Montrachet?
questions.explanation: Le Montrachet's soil is only 30-40 cm deep, sitting over hard limestone bedrock — this shallow topsoil is key to its elegant style.

questions.question: Roughly how great is the age gap between the Kimmeridgian and Portlandian soil layers?
questions.explanation: Kimmeridgian (about 155 million years ago) and Portlandian (about 150 million years ago) differ by about 5 million years, but produce distinctly different soil characteristics.

questions.question: Higher limestone content generally produces more elegant, refined wines.
questions.explanation: Soil with high limestone content (50-70%) drains extremely well and typically produces elegant, highly mineral, high-acid wines.

questions.question: Top vineyard plots are typically located where on a slope?
questions.explanation: Mid-slope is generally ideal — combining good drainage, moderate water stress, and favorable aspect, while avoiding both frost and waterlogging.

questions.question: What proportion of whole-cluster fermentation does DRC use?
questions.explanation: DRC uses 100% whole-cluster fermentation, believing it brings the greatest complexity and aging potential.

questions.question: Whole-cluster fermentation requires fully ripe stems, or it introduces green, unripe flavors.
questions.explanation: Stems must be fully ripe (turned brown and lignified); unripe green stems bring green, herbaceous off-flavors.

questions.question: Roughly what proportion of new oak does Coche-Dury use for its white wines?
questions.explanation: Coche-Dury uses only 20-30% new oak, avoiding wood flavors masking the wine's refined minerality.

questions.question: What is the capacity of a standard Burgundy oak barrel?
questions.explanation: The standard Burgundy barrel (a pièce) holds 228 liters, slightly larger than the Bordeaux barrique's 225 liters.

questions.question: Bâtonnage (lees stirring) is used mainly for white wine, and adds roundness and bread-like aromas.
questions.explanation: Bâtonnage resuspends the lees, releasing polysaccharides and flavor compounds, adding roundness to the white wine and its bread- and butter-like aromas.

questions.question: What is the main effect of malolactic fermentation (MLF)?
options: Converts malic acid to lactic acid, lowering acidity
questions.explanation: MLF converts sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, lowering total acidity by roughly 2-4 g/L and adding roundness.

questions.question: As the climate warms, some producers have begun experimenting with blocking MLF in white wines to preserve acidity.
questions.explanation: In low-acid vintages (such as 2018 and 2022), some innovative estates block MLF to preserve acidity and freshness.

questions.question: What is the typical maceration time for Burgundy red wine?
questions.explanation: Burgundy red wine typically macerates for 15-30 days — much longer than the New World — to extract a complex tannin structure.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of cold maceration?
options: Extract aroma and color without extracting tannin
questions.explanation: Cold maceration takes place at 5-10°C for 5-7 days, extracting aroma and color, but not tannin, due to the low temperature.

questions.question: Both DRC and Leroy refuse to filter their wines, believing filtration harms terroir expression.
questions.explanation: Both top estates insist on unfiltered bottling to preserve all flavor compounds and texture — though there may be sediment, the flavor is more complete.

questions.question: How many producers share ownership of the Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Clos de Vougeot is shared by more than 80 producers, making it Burgundy's most fragmented Grand Cru in terms of ownership.

questions.question: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze can be labeled as Chambertin, but not the other way around.
questions.explanation: The law allows Clos de Bèze to be labeled as Chambertin, but not vice versa — reflecting Clos de Bèze's prestige.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Gevrey-Chambertin have?
questions.explanation: Gevrey-Chambertin has 9 Grands Crus, including Chambertin, Clos de Bèze, and 7 Grands Crus bearing the Chambertin suffix.

questions.question: Where does the name Corton-Charlemagne come from?
questions.explanation: Corton-Charlemagne is named after Emperor Charlemagne, who is said to have ordered the site replanted with white grapes.

questions.question: How many white-wine Grands Crus does the Montrachet family have?
questions.explanation: The Montrachet family has 5 white-wine Grands Crus: Le Montrachet, Chevalier, Bâtard, Bienvenues-Bâtard, and Criots-Bâtard.

questions.question: Chevalier-Montrachet sits upslope of Le Montrachet and has a more elegant, refined style.
questions.explanation: Chevalier-Montrachet sits upslope with thinner soil and more limestone, producing extremely elegant, high-acid, highly mineral white wine.

questions.question: What proportion of the Musigny Grand Cru does Comte de Vogüé own?
questions.explanation: Comte de Vogüé owns about 7 of Musigny's 10.8 hectares — about 70% — making it virtually synonymous with Musigny.

questions.question: The Bonnes-Mares Grand Cru straddles the villages of Chambolle-Musigny and Morey-Saint-Denis.
questions.explanation: Bonnes-Mares is about 85% in Chambolle and 15% in Morey-Saint-Denis, with each side showing slightly different styles.

questions.question: From an investment perspective, which Grand Cru offers relatively better value?
questions.explanation: Clos de la Roche is of excellent quality but relatively underrated, with reasonable pricing and better investment value.

questions.question: The quality of Clos de Vougeot's upper-slope plots can rival which of the following?
questions.explanation: Clos de Vougeot's upper-slope plots (such as those held by Méo-Camuzet) approach Musigny-level quality, far exceeding an ordinary Grand Cru.

questions.question: Over the past 20 years, roughly what has been DRC Romanée-Conti's average annual price appreciation?
questions.explanation: According to auction data, DRC Romanée-Conti's average annual appreciation from 2000-2024 has been about 12% — far exceeding traditional investments.

questions.question: Roughly what share of global wine production does Burgundy account for?
questions.explanation: Burgundy accounts for less than 1% of global wine production, yet holds 30-40% of the fine wine market.

questions.question: Auction houses' buyer's premium is typically 15-25%.
questions.explanation: International auction houses charge buyers a 15-25% premium — an important cost to factor into the total.

questions.question: In an ideal wine investment portfolio, what share should core blue-chip wines occupy?
questions.explanation: The suggested allocation is: 70% core blue-chip (steady appreciation), 20% growth-oriented, 10% speculative.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of buying En Primeur?
options: The price is usually lower and it secures an allocation
questions.explanation: The main advantage of En Primeur is that the price is typically 10-30% lower than after bottling, and it secures an allocation, but it requires paying upfront and waiting 2-3 years.

questions.question: Building an allocation relationship with DRC typically requires 5-10 years of consistent purchasing.
questions.explanation: Allocations from top estates like DRC are extremely hard to obtain, requiring long-term purchasing and relationship-building — typically 5-10 years or more.

questions.question: Roughly what is the annual storage cost at a professional wine cellar?
questions.explanation: Professional cellar storage typically costs $50-100 per case (12 bottles) a year — about 2-3% of the wine's value.

questions.question: Roughly what share of fine Burgundy on the market has authenticity concerns?
questions.explanation: It's estimated that about 10-20% of fine wine on the market has authenticity concerns, especially for top estates like DRC — buyers need careful authentication.

questions.question: In 2022-2023, the Burgundy market saw its first price correction of about 10-15%.
questions.explanation: Affected by the global economic slowdown, the Burgundy market experienced its first correction in 2022-2023, before stabilizing from 2024 onward.

questions.question: Roughly what is the annual cost of wine collection insurance, relative to collection value?
questions.explanation: Wine collection insurance typically costs 0.5-1% of the total collection value annually — an important part of risk management.

questions.question: What temperature should an ideal wine cellar be kept at?
questions.explanation: A professional cellar should maintain a steady 12-14°C, with fluctuation no greater than ±1°C — the best temperature for long-term wine aging.

questions.question: What is the ideal humidity range for a wine cellar?
questions.explanation: Cellar humidity should be kept at 60-75% — enough to prevent corks from drying out, but not so much that labels grow mold.

questions.question: An aged Burgundy with a fill level above BN (Base Neck) is considered to be in excellent condition.
questions.explanation: A fill level at BN (Base of Neck) or IN (Into Neck) represents excellent condition — the standard for investment-grade collections.

questions.question: Roughly what share of fine wine on the market do experts estimate has authenticity concerns?
questions.explanation: It's estimated that about 10-20% of fine wine on the market has authenticity concerns, especially for top estates like DRC — buyers need to be careful.

questions.question: Roughly what is the annual premium for professional wine insurance, relative to collection value?
questions.explanation: Professional wine insurance premiums typically run 0.5-1.5% of collection value annually, depending on coverage and risk.

questions.question: Wines with complete provenance records can command a 30-50% price premium.
questions.explanation: Clear provenance greatly reduces the risk of counterfeits, so wines with complete provenance can command a significant premium.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common red flag for counterfeit wine?
questions.explanation: Clear, complete provenance is a feature of a genuine wine; the other options are all common red flags for counterfeits.

questions.question: What fill level is acceptable for a 30-year-old wine?
questions.explanation: For a 30-year-old wine, a fill level between TS (Top Shoulder) and HS (High Shoulder) is acceptable — natural evaporation is normal at this age.

questions.question: Standard homeowner's insurance is usually sufficient to cover a high-value wine collection.
questions.explanation: Standard homeowner's insurance typically doesn't cover wine, or has a very low claim cap (e.g. $5,000) — high-value collections need dedicated wine insurance.

questions.question: In what year did the Rudy Kurniawan counterfeit wine case take place?
questions.explanation: The 2012 Rudy Kurniawan case is the largest counterfeiting scandal in wine history, exposing the fine wine market's counterfeiting problem.

questions.question: What is the first thing you observe in systematic blind tasting?
questions.explanation: Systematic blind tasting follows the order "appearance → aroma → palate → conclusion," starting with color, clarity, and viscosity.

questions.question: What is typical of Gevrey-Chambertin's character?
questions.explanation: Gevrey-Chambertin is known for its powerful structure, black fruit, and gamey notes — one of the Côte d'Or's most masculine villages.

questions.question: Burgundy from a hot vintage is typically deep in color, low in acidity, and high in alcohol.
questions.explanation: In hot vintages (such as 2015 and 2019), grapes ripen fully, leading to deeper color, higher sugar (higher alcohol), and relatively lower acidity.

questions.question: What color does a 15-year-old Burgundy red typically show?
questions.explanation: A 15-year-old Burgundy evolves from ruby to brick red, with the rim starting to show orange-brown tones.

questions.question: Which producer is known for a high proportion of new oak and a modern style?
questions.explanation: Méo-Camuzet is known for a relatively high proportion of new oak (50-100%) and a polished, immediately appealing modern style.

questions.question: Whole-cluster fermentation brings spice and stem-tannin character to the wine.
questions.explanation: Whole-cluster fermentation retains the stems, bringing cinnamon, clove, and other spice aromas, along with distinctive stem tannin.

questions.question: How long does the peak drinking window of a top Burgundy red typically last?
questions.explanation: Top Burgundy's peak window (when all elements are in perfect balance) typically lasts 10-15 years before slowly declining.

questions.question: In a 100-point scale, what quality tier does a score of 90-94 typically represent?
questions.explanation: On the 100-point scale: 85-89 = Good, 90-94 = Very Good, 95-100 = Outstanding/Exceptional.

questions.question: Chambolle-Musigny is typically deeper in color and firmer in tannin than Gevrey-Chambertin.
questions.explanation: The opposite is true — Chambolle is known for its bright color, silky fine tannin, and elegant style, while Gevrey is the deep, powerful representative.

questions.question: In blind tasting, an overtly obvious vanilla and toasted-bread aroma typically suggests what?
options: A high proportion of new oak
questions.explanation: Vanilla, toasted bread, and mocha aromas come from oak; when overtly obvious, it usually indicates a high proportion (50-100%) of new barrels.

questions.question: What principle underlies the classic pairing of Chablis with oysters?
options: Contrast principle (high acid cutting through marine brininess)
questions.explanation: Chablis's high acidity and minerality balance oysters' marine brininess and richness — a contrast-based pairing principle.

questions.question: Which of the following pairings is a mistake?
questions.explanation: High-tannin red wine paired with fish produces a metallic, bitter taste — a cardinal sin of food and wine pairing.

questions.question: Meursault's full body and creamy texture suit rich, buttery-sauce dishes — this is the complementary pairing principle.
questions.explanation: Rich Meursault paired with rich, buttery sauce reinforces similar qualities — this is complementary pairing.

questions.question: What is the best pairing for the classic Burgundy dish Coq au Vin?
questions.explanation: Coq au Vin (chicken braised in red wine) is traditionally cooked with Gevrey red wine, which is also the best pairing to serve alongside it.

questions.question: Which Burgundy wine best pairs with sushi and sashimi?
questions.explanation: Chablis's minerality and high acidity match perfectly with raw fish's marine freshness — now a classic pairing.

questions.question: Spicy Sichuan and Hunan cuisine pairs well with high-tannin Burgundy red.
questions.explanation: Spice plus high tannin creates a compounding effect that makes the wine taste bitter and harsh — this pairing should be avoided.

questions.question: What is the typical pairing order for a Michelin-star tasting menu?
questions.explanation: Tasting menus follow the principle of light to heavy, white before red, finishing with a sweet wine.

questions.question: What is the best pairing for Époisses cheese (a washed-rind cheese)?
questions.explanation: Époisses has an intensely pungent flavor that needs the sweetness of a sweet white wine or the alcohol strength of Marc to balance it.

questions.question: A dish's sauce is often more important to the pairing than the main ingredient itself.
questions.explanation: The sauce usually dominates a dish's flavor, so its character matters more than the main ingredient when choosing a wine.

questions.question: What style of Burgundy best suits Wagyu beef's rich marbling?
questions.explanation: Wagyu's marbling needs silky, fine tannin to complement it — Chambolle or Vosne's elegant style suits best.

questions.question: Who founded biodynamic viticulture?
questions.explanation: Biodynamics was proposed in 1924 by the Austrian philosopher Rudolf Steiner, based on his philosophy of anthroposophy.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of Preparation 500 (horn manure)?
questions.explanation: Preparation 500 is sprayed on soil to activate soil microorganisms and promote root development.

questions.question: Biodynamics requires meeting organic farming standards first, before further certification.
questions.explanation: Biodynamic requirements are stricter than organic farming — a vineyard must first meet organic standards, then follow the additional biodynamic requirements.

questions.question: In what year did DRC begin adopting biodynamics?
questions.explanation: DRC began experimenting with biodynamics in 1985 under Aubert de Villaine's push, adopting it fully by the 1990s.

questions.question: According to biodynamic lunar theory, what is the best day for harvesting?
questions.explanation: A "fruit day" (when the moon passes through a fire sign) is considered the best day to harvest, as fruit energy is believed to be at its peak.

questions.question: Domaine Leroy's average yield is about 15-20 hl/ha, far lower than DRC's 25-30 hl/ha.
questions.explanation: Leroy pursues an extremely low-yield strategy (15-20 hl/ha), even more extreme than DRC (25-30), in pursuit of maximum concentration.

questions.question: What are the main certification bodies for biodynamic viticulture?
questions.explanation: Demeter (international) and Biodyvin (France) are the two main certification bodies for biodynamic viticulture.

questions.question: What is the scientific community's main criticism of biodynamics?
options: Lack of double-blind controlled trials confirming its claims
questions.explanation: The scientific community's main criticism of biodynamics is the lack of rigorous double-blind controlled trials; some practices (such as lunar influence) are viewed as pseudoscience.

questions.question: Preparation 501 (horn silica) is mainly sprayed on the leaves to enhance photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Preparation 501 is sprayed on the leaves and is said to enhance photosynthesis and promote fruit ripening, complementing 500 (used on soil).

questions.question: What do biodynamic practitioners believe is the key to its success?
options: The effect of a single mystical preparation
The direct influence of lunar phases
The overall management philosophy and rigorous vineyard management
Being a substitute for chemical fertilizers
questions.explanation: Even though the scientific community questions some practices, biodynamics' overall management philosophy (strict organic management, low yields, soil care) does deliver high quality.

questions.question: Over the past 50 years (1970-2020), roughly how much has Burgundy's average temperature risen?
questions.explanation: Between 1970 and 2020, Burgundy's average temperature rose about 1.8°C, higher than the global average of 1.1°C.

questions.question: Compared with the 1980s, roughly how much earlier is Burgundy's average harvest in the 2020s?
questions.explanation: The harvest has moved from late September to late August — about 30 days (over 4 weeks) earlier.

questions.question: Spring frost in 2021 caused some Burgundy areas to lose 50-80% of their yield.
questions.explanation: The April 2021 spring frost was one of the most severe recent disasters, causing heavy losses at many estates.

questions.question: What is the main effect of warming on Burgundy red wine?
questions.explanation: High temperatures cause rapid sugar accumulation (higher alcohol) and malic acid breakdown (lower acidity), altering the traditional balance.

questions.question: Which region is most likely to be a beneficiary of climate change?
questions.explanation: Chablis was historically often under-ripe; with warming it now reaches ideal ripeness while retaining high acidity — a dramatic leap in quality.

questions.question: In 2020, French regulations were relaxed to allow top-tier vineyards moderate irrigation during extreme drought.
questions.explanation: Facing climate change, 2020 regulations allow moderate irrigation in emergency situations.

questions.question: What winemaking adjustments have estates made to cope with high temperatures?
questions.explanation: Whole-cluster fermentation (retaining stems) brings tannin and acidity, helping balance the high alcohol and low acidity caused by warming.

questions.question: According to IPCC projections, roughly how much further might Burgundy warm by 2050 (moderate scenario)?
questions.explanation: Under a moderate emissions scenario, Burgundy may warm a further 1-1.5°C by 2050 — a total rise of about 3°C compared with 1970.

questions.question: The Hautes-Côtes (high-altitude areas) are rising in value due to climate change.
questions.explanation: High-altitude areas were historically too cool; now the temperature is suitable while acidity is preserved, increasing their investment value.

questions.question: What is Burgundy's most fundamental challenge in the face of climate change?
options: Preserving Pinot Noir's elegant style and terroir character
questions.explanation: High alcohol and low acidity threaten Burgundy's traditional elegant style — how to preserve Pinot Noir's character is the core challenge.

questions.question: Which auction house has the largest annual global wine trading volume?
questions.explanation: Acker Merrall & Condit is the largest US wine auction house, with annual trading volume of $150-200 million.

questions.question: What is the typical buyer's premium charged by international auction houses?
questions.explanation: The buyer's premium is typically 15-25% — the rate may be slightly lower at higher prices — an additional fee the buyer pays beyond the hammer price.

questions.question: Once you raise your paddle to bid at an auction, it is legally binding and cannot be withdrawn.
questions.explanation: Once a bid is placed, it forms a legally binding commitment — the winning bidder must pay and cannot cancel.

questions.question: What does "reserve price" mean at an auction?
options: The minimum price set by the seller
questions.explanation: The reserve price is the minimum set by the seller; the auction house will not sell the lot below this price.

questions.question: Roughly what price premium can perfect bottle condition command over average condition?
questions.explanation: Perfect bottle condition (fill level IN/BN, intact label) can command a 20-50% premium over average condition — an important price factor.

questions.question: The auction price typically includes the buyer's premium and shipping.
questions.explanation: The hammer price does not include the buyer's premium, shipping, insurance, and other costs — these are all additional.

questions.question: What is the best tool for checking historical auction prices for wine?
questions.explanation: Wine-Searcher Pro provides global retail prices and auction history data — a professional price-lookup tool.

questions.question: What does the "as-is" clause at auction mean?
options: Sold in current condition, no returns after sale
questions.explanation: "As-is" means sold in its current condition — the buyer bears the risk of bottle condition, and returns or claims aren't accepted after winning the bid.

questions.question: The preview is an important opportunity to personally inspect a lot's condition before bidding.
questions.explanation: The preview lets buyers personally inspect bottle condition, label, and fill level — especially important for high-value lots, and worth attending whenever possible.

questions.question: What is the most common mistake made by novice bidders?
options: Getting emotional and bidding beyond budget
questions.explanation: Novices most often lose their composure in intense bidding and emotionally chase a lot beyond their budget — the mistake to avoid most.

questions.question: What is the top score in the Parker rating system?
questions.explanation: Robert Parker uses a 100-point scale, with the actual range running 50-100, though most wines fall between 85 and 100.

questions.question: When describing Burgundy red wine color, what does "garnet" refer to?
questions.explanation: Garnet is the typical color of Burgundy Pinot Noir entering its drinking window, between the young Ruby and the aged Tawny.

questions.question: Primary aromas refer to those coming from the grape variety itself.
questions.explanation: Primary aromas come from the grape variety, secondary aromas from winemaking, and tertiary aromas from aging.

questions.question: In Allen Meadows' (Burghound's) scoring system, what does a score above 96 represent?
questions.explanation: A Burghound score above 96 is extremely rare, given only to the greatest wines of the greatest vintages — fewer than 10 wines a year.

questions.question: In the WSET tasting system, what does SAT stand for?
questions.explanation: SAT is WSET's abbreviation for "Systematic Approach to Tasting."

questions.question: In tannin description, "fine-grained" refers to coarse tannin.
questions.explanation: "Fine-grained" refers to refined tannin — a feature of high-quality wine. Coarse tannin is described as "coarse" or "rough."

questions.question: In tasting notes, how long does a "long finish" typically last?
questions.explanation: A "long finish" typically means over 15 seconds. A short finish is under 3 seconds, and a medium finish is 6-12 seconds.

questions.question: When describing body, how is a Burgundy Grand Cru typically characterized?
questions.explanation: Burgundy Grand Cru is typically Medium+ to Full body — more structured and concentrated than a Village-level Medium body.

questions.question: Professional tasting notes should avoid any subjective emotional expression.
questions.explanation: While technical description should be the main focus, a measured degree of personal impression (especially in a "personal notes" section) can add authenticity and reference value. The key is distinguishing objective description from subjective impression.

questions.question: What is CellarTracker's main function?
questions.explanation: CellarTracker is the world's largest tasting-note and cellar-management platform, offering free logging, tracking, and community ratings.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Burgundy have in total?
questions.explanation: Burgundy has 33 Grands Crus in total: 24 in the Côte de Nuits (red), 8 white + 1 red (Corton) in the Côte de Beaune, and 7 (white) in Chablis.

questions.question: Roughly how large is DRC's Romanée-Conti monopole?
questions.explanation: The Romanée-Conti monopole is about 1.8 hectares, producing about 6,000 bottles a year — one of the world's most expensive wines.

questions.question: When planning a Burgundy estate visit, top estates like DRC and Leroy typically require booking 6 months in advance.
questions.explanation: Booking visits at top estates is extremely difficult, requiring 6 months or more lead time, and usually an introduction through a négociant or industry professional.

questions.question: When building a balanced Burgundy collection, what share of the total budget should investment-grade wines occupy?
questions.explanation: Investment-grade wines are recommended to make up 20-30% of the budget, with 50% for everyday and special-occasion wines — maintaining a balanced pyramid structure.

questions.question: In fine-dining wine-list design, what is the main advantage of by-the-glass pours?
options: Lowers the barrier to purchase and boosts margins
questions.explanation: By-the-glass lowers the barrier for guests to try expensive wine, and since one bottle yields 5 glasses, margins can reach 75-80% — higher than bottle sales.

questions.question: Allen Meadows (Burghound) scores above 96 are extremely rare — fewer than 10 wines get one per year.
questions.explanation: Burghound scores above 96 are extremely rare, given only to the greatest wines of the greatest vintages — one of Burgundy's strictest rating standards.

questions.question: Which wine set the world record for a single bottle at auction in 2018?
questions.explanation: In October 2018, a bottle of 1945 DRC Romanée-Conti sold at Sotheby's for $558,000, setting the world record for a single bottle of wine at auction.

questions.question: When pricing a restaurant wine list, what is the suggested markup multiple for a mid-tier wine (cost NT$5-10K)?
questions.explanation: A mid-tier wine is suggested to be priced at 3.0-3.2x cost, achieving 67-69% margin — competitive while maintaining reasonable profit.

questions.question: When building a collection, you should concentrate purchases in a single great vintage (like 2015) for the best investment return.
questions.explanation: You should diversify vintage risk instead — a suggested mix is 30% great vintages, 50% good vintages, and 20% early-drinking vintages, avoiding concentration risk in a single vintage's market.

questions.question: After completing the Level 3 course, which advanced professional certification is most suitable?
questions.explanation: Level 3 graduates are well-suited to challenge the WSET Level 3 Award or the CMS Certified Sommelier (Level 2) as a starting point for advanced professional certification.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Chablis have in total?
questions.explanation: Chablis has 7 Grands Crus in total: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, and Vaudésir.

questions.question: The Coravin system lets restaurants sell high-value wine by the glass without affecting quality.
questions.explanation: The Coravin system uses inert gas to pour wine without removing the cork, preserving quality for weeks or even months, making by-the-glass service of expensive wines possible.

questions.question: What is the best way to build a long-term purchasing relationship in Burgundy?
options: Become a VIP client of a merchant and buy regularly
Switch merchants every time to compare prices
questions.explanation: Becoming a long-term VIP client gets you priority access to allocated wines, expert advice, and better pricing — the best strategy for building a collection.

questions.question: At auction, what does the buyer's premium typically run, relative to the hammer price?
questions.explanation: The buyer's premium is typically 15-25% — an additional cost the buyer pays to the auction house beyond the hammer price, sometimes slightly lower at higher prices.

questions.question: The Level 3 course covers a complete Burgundy knowledge system, from beginner to professional level.
questions.explanation: The Level 3 course integrates terroir, history, producers, investment, tasting, and business application to build a professional-level Burgundy knowledge system.
